title: Attract the Right Construction Clients, Not Just More Leads
meta_description: How to attract better construction clients: track where your leads come from, diversify past word of mouth, and pitch so architects and developers listen.
h1: Attract the Right Construction Clients, Not Just More Leads
hero_subtitle: A practical guide to winning higher value work from developers and architects.

intro.answer: Word of mouth gets a construction business started. It rarely gets one to the next level, because it brings you the same conversions, odd jobs and refurbishments you were already getting.

image.alt: A builder meeting an architect on site to discuss a higher value construction project

intro.roadmap: This guide covers three ways to improve where your clients come from: tracking your lead sources so you can see what actually works, diversifying before a single source dries up, and changing the pitch so developers and architects hear what is in it for them.

briefing.title: Track Where Your Best Clients Came From
briefing.intro: Most builders can name their biggest client. Very few can say which source produced them, or what has happened to that source since. Without that, you cannot tell whether a quiet month is bad luck or a channel closing.

panels.heading: How do you find out where your best construction clients come from?
paragraphs: Ask every person who enquires how they heard about you, and record the answer. A spreadsheet is enough to start with. A CRM is better once the volume justifies it.

Look at total enquiries each month, then break them down by source. One of Greg's own businesses used to get steady work from the council. Tracking showed leads dropping off across August and September. A conversation revealed budget cuts. Because the trend was spotted early, there was time to diversify rather than react.

panels.heading: Diversify before a source dries up
paragraphs: LinkedIn is where several of Greg's coaching clients have found higher value work. The sequence matters more than the effort.
steps: Fix the profile first. A photo of you, not just a logo. An About section naming your expertise, your key services and the value of the jobs you want.
Search for the client type you want, filter by area, and filter to people who have posted in the last month so you are reaching active accounts.
Build a shortlist of 10 to 30 names rather than messaging everyone.
Lead with what the project needs, not with how long you have been established.

review.label: Review monthly
review.text: Enquiries by source, and which sources produced the work worth having. A source that is trending down for two months in a row is a decision, not a blip.

append_sections.heading: How can UK builders win higher-value contracts without taking on the wrong work?
paragraphs: A higher-value contract is one that supports profit, cash flow and reliable delivery, not simply a larger contract price. Clear scope and workable payment stages can make a smaller job a better fit than a larger project that stretches the team.

Test four things. Capacity: can the right people and trades do it without harming existing clients? Job contribution: after direct costs, supervision, defects and disruption, does it improve the business? Cash exposure: do payment terms, retention and materials leave the builder funding the work? Ability to deliver: can the builder meet the client's quality, programme and communication needs?

Example: a larger refurbishment with unclear scope and late payment may look attractive, but a smaller job with a clear brief, staged payments and realistic dates can contribute more and protect reputation.
steps: Go or no-go checklist: confirm the client and decision maker are clear.
Check scope, drawings, approvals and site information are sufficient to price and build.
Match start and duration against current and known future workload.
Review payment terms, retention and materials against cash available.
Say no or ask for changes when a key risk is unresolved.

append_sections.heading: What evidence helps an architect or developer shortlist a builder?
paragraphs: Make it easy for an architect or developer to check relevant completed work. Explain your actual role and scope, including work delivered by others, and only share material you have permission to use.

Offer references from people who saw the work. Describe relevant constraints, such as occupied sites or restricted access, and explain how you managed changes, quality checks and aftercare. If project details are confidential, use another approved example.
steps: Provide a short list of completed jobs relevant to the project type and size.
State the actual role, scope and subcontractor involvement.
Confirm permission for every client name, image, drawing or reference.
Offer references who can speak to delivery, communication and aftercare.
Name constraints and how they were managed, and show examples of quality control and defect close-out.
